Woebegone means looking deeply sad, miserable, and sorrowful — often in a way that is clearly visible on a person's face or in their whole appearance.

The key idea here is visible sadness. When you call someone woebegone, you are not just saying they feel sad inside. You are saying their sadness is written all over them — in their drooping eyes, their slumped shoulders, their pale and tired face, their defeated posture. The sorrow has taken over their entire appearance.

Think of it this way: if you walked into a room and saw a person sitting alone, shoulders hunched, eyes downcast, face long and heavy — that person looks woebegone.

The kind of sadness woebegone describes is not the sharp, explosive kind — like someone crying loudly or screaming in grief. It is quieter and heavier than that. It is the look of someone who has been worn down by sorrow, someone who seems weighed down and depleted. There is a sense of helplessness and misery in it — a kind of "I have been beaten by life right now" quality.

It can also suggest that the sadness has been going on for a while, not just a passing moment of disappointment.
How It Compares to Similar Words

English has many words for sadness. Here is how woebegone sits among them:

  • Sad — the most general word. It just means unhappy, nothing more.
  • Miserable — stronger than sad. Focuses on how terrible the person feels inside.
  • Dejected — means downcast and dispirited, like someone who has lost hope or confidence.
  • Forlorn — means lonely and abandoned-feeling sad, like someone left behind.
  • Woebegone — focuses specifically on the visible, outward appearance of deep sadness. It is the word you reach for when you want to paint a picture of how someone looks, not just state that they feel bad.

So if you say "she felt miserable," you are telling us about her inner state. But if you say "she looked woebegone," you are showing us her face and her whole body — the visible portrait of her misery.
Who or What Can Be Woebegone?

People are the most common subject. A person's face, eyes, or expression can be woebegone. A person's entire figure or appearance can be woebegone.

Animals can also be described this way. A dog waiting by the door for an owner who hasn't come home can have a woebegone face — that classic sad-puppy look.

Places and things can sometimes be described as woebegone too, though less often. A run-down, neglected, and bleak-looking building or neighbourhood can be called woebegone — as if the place itself looks sad and abandoned. This is a more poetic or extended use of the word.

Woebegone is a slightly literary word. You are more likely to find it in books, stories, and careful writing than in everyday casual conversation. It gives writing a vivid, evocative quality — when an author writes that a character looks woebegone, it paints an instant picture.

It can be used in two tones:

  1. With sympathy — genuinely noting that someone looks deeply sad and pitiful. "The young boy stood at the gate with a woebegone expression, and my heart broke for him."
  2. With gentle humour — sometimes used in a slightly playful or ironic way to describe someone who is dramatically sad over something minor. "He wore a woebegone face for the rest of the evening just because his team lost a game." Here, the word gently pokes fun at the exaggerated display of misery.

• After hearing the bad news, she sat quietly in the corner, her face utterly woebegone.
  • The abandoned dog looked up at me with such woebegone eyes that I couldn't walk away.
  • He returned from the trip looking tired and woebegone, as though something had broken inside him.
  • The old neighbourhood had a woebegone appearance — peeling paint, broken fences, and empty streets.
  • She gave me a woebegone look, and I immediately knew something had gone very wrong.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: woebegone = visibly and deeply sad in a way that shows all over a person's face and body. It is sadness you can see.
